subject: nlp
title: Practice bank: Lecture 1 (Basic processing)
description: New quiz-style practice questions on Lecture 1 (tokenization, morphology, one-hot vectors, the distributional hypothesis and count-based methods), with co-occurrence and PPMI calculations. Written for exam revision from the slides and the tutorial. Not from the lecturer: the answers are unofficial.
negativeMarkingNote: The real Moodle quiz uses negative marking on MCQ questions: picking all right and wrong answers on a question results in a mark of 0.

questions.question: Tokenizing "The children are selling the clothes to each other." by splitting on white space and punctuation gives how many tokens?
questions.explanation: The slide's own example: ["The", "children", "are", "selling", "the", "clothes", "to", "each", "other", "."]: the full stop is its own token.

questions.question: True or False: For many African languages tokenization is non-trivial because they are agglutinative: one written word can contain a subject marker, tense, object marker, verb root and more.
questions.explanation: The slide splits "Abashana bayazithengiselana izimpahla" into many morphemes ("Aba-shana ba-ya-zi-theng-is-el-an-a"). Whitespace splitting leaves huge, rare words.

questions.question: Why does whitespace tokenization work worse for isiZulu than for English?
choices: Words are agglutinative, so each whitespace "word" packs several morphemes and most word forms are rare
isiZulu has no spaces between words
isiZulu words are always shorter than English words
questions.explanation: A whitespace token in isiZulu often corresponds to a whole English clause, so the vocabulary explodes and most words are seen rarely. This returns in L4 (BPE) and L10 (tokenizers for African languages).

questions.question: Which output is typical of stemming rather than lemmatization?
questions.explanation: Stemming chops off endings with crude heuristics, so it can produce non-words. Mapping "ran" → "run" or "better" → "good" needs a vocabulary and morphological analysis: lemmatization.

questions.question: True or False: Lemmatization uses a vocabulary and morphological analysis, normally aiming to remove inflectional endings only and return the dictionary form (the lemma).
questions.explanation: The slide's definition: runs, running, ran → run.

questions.question: Which statements about stemming and lemmatization are true?
choices: Both aim to reduce inflectional (and sometimes derivationally related) forms to a common base form
Lemmatization returns a dictionary word (the lemma)
Stemming always returns a valid dictionary word
"car, cars, car's, cars'" → "car" is an example of this kind of reduction
questions.explanation: Stemming is a crude heuristic and can produce non-words.

questions.question: Which of these is a bound morpheme?
questions.explanation: A bound morpheme does not occur on its own in the language; "-ness" only appears attached to a root or stem.

questions.question: True or False: An unbound (free) morpheme is one that can be found on its own in the language.
questions.explanation: For example "kind" or "come". Roots, stems and affixes are other morpheme types.

questions.question: Match each term to its definition (Lecture 1).

pairs.answer: The smallest meaningful unit of grammar
A bound morpheme combined with a root or stem
A root plus derivational affixes, without inflectional affixes
The study of how morphemes are placed together
The rules of how to combine words to form sentences

options: The smallest meaningful unit of grammar
A bound morpheme combined with a root or stem
A root plus derivational affixes, without inflectional affixes
The study of how morphemes are placed together
The rules of how to combine words to form sentences
questions.explanation: From the terminology slides.

questions.question: Which pair is an example of inflection rather than derivation?
questions.explanation: Inflection usually keeps the word class and is required by grammar ("comes" is still a verb). Derivation forms a new word and usually changes the class (adjective → noun).

questions.question: Which statements about derivation and inflection are true?
choices: Derivation forms a new word or stem, usually changing the word class
Inflection changes meaning in a predictable way and is invoked by grammar (obligatory)
Inflection usually changes a noun into a verb
questions.explanation: Changing the word class is typical of derivation, not inflection.

questions.question: What is a corpus?
choices: A computer-readable collection of text or speech
A single sentence used for testing
questions.explanation: Plural: corpora (slide 15).

questions.question: True or False: The data a BPE tokenizer is trained on (its corpus) does not have to be the same data used to train the model.
questions.explanation: L4 slide 37: the tokenizer's input is "a corpus of text to train the tokenizer, not necessarily the same data we use to train our model".

questions.question: With a vocabulary of 50,000 words, what is the cosine similarity between the one-hot vectors of "cat" and "kitten"?
questions.explanation: Different one-hot vectors are orthogonal, so their dot product (and cosine) is 0 for every pair: one-hot vectors capture no similarity of meaning.

questions.question: Which are problems with one-hot word vectors?
choices: Their size equals the vocabulary size
Every pair of words is equally (dis)similar
They cannot be fed into a linear layer
questions.explanation: A one-hot vector times a weight matrix selects a row: that is exactly an embedding lookup (Quiz 1 Q19).

questions.question: The "Tej" example (A bottle of ___ is on the table; ___ makes you drunk; we make ___ out of honey) shows that:
choices: We can infer a word's meaning from the contexts it appears in
Words have no meaning outside a dictionary
questions.explanation: Tej is an alcoholic drink made from honey: you can work this out from its contexts alone. Rows of the context table that are similar (Tej and wine) belong to words with similar meaning.

questions.question: True or False: Count-based methods first build a word–context matrix and then reduce its dimensionality, because the raw matrix is huge and sparse.
questions.explanation: Slides 33–35: (1) construct the matrix, (2) reduce its dimensionality (e.g. truncated SVD), because of size and sparsity.

questions.question:
Use the corpus "I saw a cute grey cat. a loving, cute cat" with punctuation removed (so the tokens are: I saw a cute grey cat a loving cute cat). The context of a word is the words up to 2 positions to its left and right.
Give the co-occurrence counts (a) $N(cat, cute)$, (b) $N(cute, a)$, (c) $N(grey, saw)$, (d) $N(a, cute)$.
questions.solution:
Positions: 1 I, 2 saw, 3 a, 4 cute, 5 grey, 6 cat, 7 a, 8 loving, 9 cute, 10 cat.
(a) Both "cat"s have "cute" within 2 positions (position 4 for the cat at 6; position 9 for the cat at 10): 2.
(b) "cute" at 4 has "a" at 3; "cute" at 9 has "a" at 7: 2.
(c) "grey" at 5 sees positions 3–7; "saw" is at 2: 0.
(d) 2: the matrix is symmetric for a symmetric window.
questions.explanation: This is the slide's toy corpus; check your full table against the finished one on slide 42.

questions.question: True or False: In a co-occurrence matrix with a symmetric window, $N(w, c) = N(c, w)$.
questions.explanation: Each time $c$ is within $L$ words of $w$, $w$ is within $L$ words of $c$.

questions.question:
A word–context count matrix has rows (words) w1, w2, w3 and columns (contexts) c1, c2, c3:
$$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$$
Using $\text{PMI}(w, c) = \log_2 \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)P(c)}$ with probabilities from the counts, and $\text{PPMI} = \max(0, \text{PMI})$ (0 for zero counts), give (a) PPMI(w1, c1), (b) PPMI(w1, c2), (c) PPMI(w3, c3).
questions.explanation: PPMI is in Tutorial 1.4, not on the slides (L2 recommends a PMI reading). PMI compares how often $w$ and $c$ co-occur with how often they would by chance; negative values are unreliable with sparse counts, so they are clipped to 0.

questions.question: Why is PPMI often used instead of raw co-occurrence counts?
choices: Raw counts are dominated by frequent words such as "the"; PMI measures whether two words co-occur more than chance
PPMI turns the matrix into one-hot vectors
questions.explanation: Frequent function words co-occur with everything. PMI divides by what independence predicts, and PPMI clips unreliable negative values to 0.
